```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
pal <- c("#444444", "#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#b23b3b", "#9aa7b0")
old <- options(pdmS7.user = "Ann Custodian", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
f0 <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
```

Large-sample hydrology studies a method over many catchments at once, so that a pattern is
not mistaken for the quirk of one river. Its weakness is that the truth is never known: a
calibration that scores well may still have the wrong parameters, and nothing in the record
says so.

A large sample of synthetic catchments removes that weakness. Every catchment has its own
climate and its own true model, every truth is written down, and the same automatic
calibration a real study would use is run over all of them. This article does that for 30
catchments and asks three questions:

1. How well does automatic calibration fit, on data it saw and data it did not?
2. Which parameters does it recover, and which does it not?
3. What decides whether a parameter can be recovered?

# The sample

`synthetic_basins()` writes one folder per catchment, in the layout `calibrate_batch()` reads.
Each catchment draws its own climate (how wet, how stormy, how much evaporation) and its own
true parameters, within the calibration bounds. Each record is ten years of daily data,
gauged with persistent error and an extrapolated rating above its highest gauging.

```{r sample}
basins <- file.path(tempdir(), "sample-basins")
output <- file.path(tempdir(), "sample-projects")
unlink(c(basins, output), recursive = TRUE)
sample <- synthetic_basins(basins, n = 30, years = 10, dt = 24, seed = 7)
round(sapply(sample[, c("area_km2", "rain_mm", "pet_mm", "cmax", "kg", "k1", "kb")],
             range), 1)
```

```{r climate, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="The sample's climates and catchments. Left: annual rain against potential evaporation. Right: soil capacity against recharge time constant. Each point is one catchment."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.8, 0.8))
plot(sample$pet_mm, sample$rain_mm, pch = 16, col = pal[2], xlab = "PET (mm a year)",
     ylab = "Rain (mm a year)")
plot(sample$cmax, sample$kg, log = "y", pch = 16, col = pal[3], xlab = "cmax (mm)",
     ylab = "kg (hours, log scale)")
```

The sample spans rain from `r f0(min(sample$rain_mm))` to `r f0(max(sample$rain_mm))` mm a
year, areas from `r f0(min(sample$area_km2))` to `r f0(max(sample$area_km2))` km2, and soil
capacities from `r f0(min(sample$cmax))` to `r f0(max(sample$cmax))` mm. Climate and
catchment are drawn independently, as they would not be in nature, so that their effects
can be told apart.

# Calibrating all of them

One call calibrates the whole sample: automatic calibration of all seven parameters at once
from the standard preset, with four starts, in parallel workers. Each record's two wettest
years are held back and revealed at the end by the test, as every project does by default.

```{r batch}
# R CMD check allows two processes; elsewhere use up to four cores. The results do not depend
# on the number: each basin's random starts are seeded from its name.
limited <- identical(toupper(Sys.getenv("_R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_")), "TRUE")
cores <- if (limited) 2L else min(4L, max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L))
elapsed <- system.time(
  calibrate_batch(basins, output, starts = 4, control = list(maxit = 40), cores = cores,
                  test = TRUE)
)[["elapsed"]]
status <- batch_status(output)
table(status$state)
results <- batch_results(output)
```

```{r batch-numbers, include=FALSE}
minutes <- elapsed / 60
```

All `r sum(status$state == "done")` catchments finished, in `r f0(minutes)` minutes on
`r cores` cores. A sample of hundreds takes the same call; `calibrate_batch()` resumes where
it stopped if interrupted. [Calibrating many catchments](many-catchments.html) covers
running it for real.

# How well does it fit?

```{r scores, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="The share of catchments reaching each score, on the calibration window, the validation window and the held-back wettest years."}
scores <- list(calibration = results$candidate_score, validation = results$validation_score,
               `wettest years` = results$wettest_score)
plot(NA, xlim = range(unlist(scores), na.rm = TRUE), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "NSE",
     ylab = "Share of catchments at or below")
for (i in seq_along(scores)) {
  lines(stats::ecdf(scores[[i]]), col = pal[i + 1], lwd = 2, do.points = FALSE)
}
legend("topleft", names(scores), col = pal[2:4], lwd = 2, bty = "n")
round(sapply(scores, stats::quantile, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), na.rm = TRUE), 3)
```

```{r score-numbers, include=FALSE}
med <- vapply(scores, stats::median, 0, na.rm = TRUE)
worst <- results$project[which.min(results$validation_score)]
```

The median catchment scores `r f3(med[["calibration"]])` on calibration,
`r f3(med[["validation"]])` on validation and `r f3(med[["wettest years"]])` on the held-back
wettest years. By the usual standard every one of these is an excellent fit. The weakest on
validation is `r worst`, at `r f3(min(results$validation_score))`. If scores were the whole
story, this would be the end of the article.

# Which parameters does it recover?

Every calibrated value can be set against its truth. The two surface stores of a cascade can
swap without changing the flow, so they are compared as the faster and the slower of the
pair.

```{r recovery}
fitted_config <- function(id) {
  project <- file.path(output, id)
  read_entry(project, read_projects(project)$candidate)$configuration
}
values <- function(cfg) {
  k <- sort(c(cfg$surface$k1, cfg$surface$k2))
  c(fc = cfg$fc, cmax = cfg$distribution$cmax, b = cfg$distribution$b,
    kg = cfg$recharge$kg, k_fast = k[1], k_slow = k[2], kb = cfg$groundwater$kb)
}
truth <- t(vapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  values(read_pdm_config(file.path(basins, id, "truth.yml")))
}, numeric(7)))
fitted <- t(vapply(sample$basin, function(id) values(fitted_config(id)), numeric(7)))
# The typical error is the median, across catchments, of the size of the error as a factor:
# 0.1 means the fitted value is typically about 10 per cent off, either way.
typical <- apply(abs(log(fitted / truth)), 2, stats::median)
data.frame(parameter = names(typical), typical_error = round(exp(typical) - 1, 3),
           within_10_percent = colSums(abs(log(fitted / truth)) < log(1.1)),
           row.names = NULL)
```

```{r recovery-plot, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Calibrated against true values, one point per catchment. Points on the line are exact. Log scales for the parameters that span orders of magnitude."}
logged <- c("kg", "k_fast", "k_slow", "kb")
par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 1.6, 0.6), cex.main = 1)
for (p in colnames(truth)) {
  lim <- range(c(truth[, p], fitted[, p]))
  plot(truth[, p], fitted[, p], log = if (p %in% logged) "xy" else "", xlim = lim, ylim = lim,
       pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(pal[2], 0.7), xlab = "true", ylab = "calibrated", main = p)
  abline(0, 1, col = pal[7], lty = 2, untf = TRUE)
}
```

```{r ranking, include=FALSE}
order_by <- names(sort(typical))
pct <- function(p) f0(100 * (exp(typical[[p]]) - 1))
```

```{r edges, include=FALSE}
# A calibrated value within 1 per cent of a bound (in logs for log-scaled parameters) means the
# search ended against the fence rather than at an optimum inside it.
b <- calibration_bounds(pdm_presets("standard"))
at_edge <- vapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  cfg <- fitted_config(id)
  v <- vapply(b$path, function(p) pdmS7:::.path_get(cfg, p), numeric(1))
  lo <- ifelse(b$scale == "log", log(b$lower), b$lower)
  hi <- ifelse(b$scale == "log", log(b$upper), b$upper)
  x <- ifelse(b$scale == "log", log(v), v)
  any(x - lo < 0.01 * (hi - lo) | hi - x < 0.01 * (hi - lo))
}, logical(1))
edge_ids <- names(at_edge)[at_edge]
```

`r if (length(edge_ids)) paste0(length(edge_ids), " calibration", if (length(edge_ids) > 1) "s" else "", " (", paste(edge_ids, collapse = ", "), ") ended with a parameter against a bound. That is worth checking in a real study: it can mean a search that went astray, or a true value close to the bound. Nothing in the batch flags it yet, so check for it as this article does.") else "No calibration ended with a parameter against a bound."`

The ranking is clear. `r order_by[1]` and `r order_by[2]` come back closest, typically within
`r pct(order_by[1])` and `r pct(order_by[2])` per cent. `r order_by[7]` and `r order_by[6]`
are the worst, typically `r pct(order_by[7])` and `r pct(order_by[6])` per cent out. Yet the
calibrations that got them wrong still score an excellent NSE. A good score shows that the
model reproduces the record; it does not show that the parameters are right.

# Did the search find the best fit?

A parameter that comes back wrong has two possible causes. The search may have stopped short
of the best fit, or the record may not be able to tell the true value from the wrong one.
The truth settles which: score each catchment's true parameters on the same calibration
window, and set the calibration's score against it.

```{r against-truth}
true_score <- vapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  project <- file.path(output, id)
  entries <- read_project(project)$entries
  fit <- utils::tail(entries$id[entries$type == "auto_calibration"], 1)
  cfg <- read_pdm_config(file.path(basins, id, "truth.yml"))
  changes <- vapply(b$path, function(p) pdmS7:::.path_get(cfg, p), numeric(1))
  suppressWarnings(preview_trial(project, fit, changes))$scores$nse
}, numeric(1))
calibrated_score <- results$candidate_score[match(sample$basin, results$project)]
gap <- calibrated_score - true_score
round(c(at_least_truth = sum(gap >= -1e-6), short_by_over_0.001 = sum(gap < -0.001),
        largest_shortfall = max(0, -min(gap))), 4)
```

```{r truth-numbers, include=FALSE}
n_match <- sum(gap >= -1e-6)
n_short <- sum(gap < -0.001)
```

In `r n_match` of the `r length(gap)` catchments the calibration scores at least as well as
the true parameters`r if (n_short == 0) paste0(", and in the rest it falls short by no more than ", sprintf("%.4f", max(0, -min(gap))), " in NSE") else paste0("; in ", n_short, " it falls short by more than 0.001")`.
`r if (n_short == 0) paste0("The search found the best fit each record allows. So when ", order_by[7], " comes back ", pct(order_by[7]), " per cent out, the search is not to blame: parameter sets that far apart fit the record equally well, and the record, with its gauge error, cannot choose between them. More model runs, or a different search, would not recover it.") else "Those catchments are search failures, and their parameters say nothing about what the record can recover."`

Two other searches were tried on this sample. Calibrating in stages (the water balance first,
then the fast response, then a joint polish) did no better, and dynamically dimensioned
search, given the same number of model runs, did worse. `inst/benchmarks/search_methods.R` in
the package runs that comparison.

# What decides whether a parameter can be recovered?

A parameter can be recovered only if the record exercises it. A natural guess is that the soil
capacity is pinned best where the climate works the soil hardest: in a dry climate the soil
fills and empties far enough for its size to show, while in a wet one many capacities fit the
record equally well. A simple measure of how hard the climate works the soil is its dryness,
potential evaporation over rain. The sample can test the guess.

```{r dryness, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="The error in each catchment's calibrated soil capacity against the dryness of its climate."}
dryness <- sample$pet_mm / sample$rain_mm
cmax_error <- abs(log(fitted[, "cmax"] / truth[, "cmax"]))
plot(dryness, cmax_error, pch = 16, col = pal[3], xlab = "Dryness (PET / rain)",
     ylab = "cmax error (|log ratio|)")
rho <- stats::cor(dryness, cmax_error, method = "spearman")
round(rho, 2)
```

```{r rho-numbers, include=FALSE}
direction <- if (rho < -0.3) "drier" else if (rho > 0.3) "wetter" else NULL
```

`r if (!is.null(direction)) paste0("Across the sample, the soil capacity is recovered better in ", direction, " climates (Spearman correlation ", f2(rho), " between dryness and the size of the error).") else paste0("Across this sample, dryness alone does not explain how well the soil capacity is recovered (Spearman correlation ", f2(rho), "): other things, such as how the parameters trade off against each other, matter as much.")`
A real large-sample study can ask the same question of its own results, but cannot see the
error itself; here it can.

# The largest floods

The test also revealed each record's two wettest years. Their peaks are above the highest
gauging, where the rating records them low, so the recorded peak is not the truth. Here the
true peak is known.

```{r peaks}
peak_rows <- lapply(sample$basin, function(id) {
  project <- file.path(output, id)
  entries <- read_project(project)$entries
  test <- read_entry(project, utils::tail(entries$id[entries$type == "test"], 1))
  forcing <- data.table::fread(file.path(basins, id, "forcing.csv"))
  forcing$time <- as.POSIXct(forcing$time, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
  true_flow <- synthetic_catchment(forcing, read_pdm_config(file.path(basins, id, "truth.yml")),
                                   error = list(sd = 0, memory_h = 72))$true_flow
  reg <- read_entry(project, entries$id[entries$type == "data_registered"][1])
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(test$wettest$years), function(i) {
    y <- test$wettest$years[[i]]
    span <- reg$scorecard$wettest$years[[i]]
    data.frame(basin = id, recorded = y$observed_peak_m3s, calibrated = y$simulated_peak_m3s,
               true = max(true_flow[span$first_row:span$last_row]),
               low = y$spread_low_m3s, high = y$spread_high_m3s)
  }))
})
peaks <- do.call(rbind, peak_rows)
vs_recorded <- peaks$calibrated / peaks$recorded - 1
vs_true <- peaks$calibrated / peaks$true - 1
round(c(median_error_vs_recorded = stats::median(vs_recorded),
        median_error_vs_true = stats::median(vs_true),
        median_spread = stats::median((peaks$high - peaks$low) / peaks$true),
        share_true_inside_spread = mean(peaks$true >= peaks$low & peaks$true <= peaks$high)), 3)
```

```{r peak-plot, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Peak error in the held-back wettest years, judged against the recorded peak (which the rating understates) and against the true peak."}
boxplot(list(`against recorded peak` = 100 * vs_recorded, `against true peak` = 100 * vs_true),
        horizontal = TRUE, col = adjustcolor(pal[2:3], 0.4), xlab = "Peak error (per cent)",
        las = 1, cex.axis = 0.85)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = pal[7])
```

```{r peak-numbers, include=FALSE}
inside <- mean(peaks$true >= peaks$low & peaks$true <= peaks$high)
```

Judged against the recorded peaks, the calibrated models look
`r f0(abs(100 * stats::median(vs_recorded)))` per cent
`r if (stats::median(vs_recorded) > 0) "high" else "low"` in the median year. Judged against
the true peaks, they are `r f0(abs(100 * stats::median(vs_true)))` per cent
`r if (stats::median(vs_true) > 0) "high" else "low"`. Across the
`r nrow(peaks)` held-back years, the range of the equally good fits contains the true peak in
`r f0(100 * inside)` per cent of them. [Larger floods](extrapolation.html) explains these
checks for one catchment; across a sample, they show how far a method can be trusted with
floods it has not seen.

# What the sample shows

- **Scores are not evidence of correct parameters.** Every catchment scored an NSE of at
  least `r f2(min(results$validation_score))` on validation. Some parameters were still
  recovered poorly, and only the known truth shows it.
- **The search is not the limit.** In `r n_match` of `r length(gap)` catchments the
  calibration fitted at least as well as the truth. What the record cannot recover, no search
  will.
- **Some parameters are reliably recovered and some are not.** Here `r order_by[1]` and
  `r order_by[2]` were within 10 per cent in `r min(colSums(abs(log(fitted / truth)) < log(1.1))[order_by[1:2]])`
  or more of the `r nrow(truth)` catchments; `r order_by[7]` was within 10 per cent in
  only `r colSums(abs(log(fitted / truth)) < log(1.1))[[order_by[7]]]` of them. A study that
  reads meaning into a parameter should first know which kind it is.
- **A rating extrapolated above the highest gauging makes a good model look bad on the
  biggest floods.** Judge peak errors with the rating flag in mind.
- **Simple explanations need testing.** The guess that dry climates pin the soil store better
  was `r if (identical(direction, "drier")) "borne out" else "not borne out"` here; a large sample is
  where such guesses are tested.
- **Large samples answer questions single catchments cannot**: which parameters to trust,
  under which climates, and how much a calibration method can be relied on beyond its record.

For a real study, replace `synthetic_basins()` with real basin folders and keep everything
else. Running a synthetic sample alongside, made to resemble the real catchments with
`fit_rain()` and sensible ranges, shows how far the method can be trusted before the real
results are read.

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
options(old)
unlink(c(basins, output), recursive = TRUE)
```
